stories.author: ggcr
summaryZh: DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale. Supported models:

comments.author: schneehertz
comments.textZhHtml:
A nuclear bomb

"Based on this framework, we have achieved high-throughput, low-latency large-scale inference services for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Currently, the service throughput of a single cluster is 155 trillion tokens/day, and the overall revenue is $38 per card per hour (at off-peak pricing)"

Source: https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2095560295930508953

comments.author: abound
comments.textZhHtml:
It's really refreshing to put some cold hard numbers on this stuff, hopefully this quells some of the "AI is unprofitable everyone is spending a dollar to make fifty cents" arguments. Amortized cost of owning a DC full of GPUs is far less than $38/card/hr

Not to say it can't still be a bubble, just that there is legitimately profit to be had and perhaps some sustainable equilibrium in the future.

comments.author: Closi
comments.textZhHtml:
> hopefully this quells some of the "AI is unprofitable everyone is spending a dollar to make fifty cents" arguments.

I think everyone has known that inference is profitable overall for the major providers for a while (I'm sure not all user accounts, but in aggregate).

The major providers are unprofitable after you add in the training and research costs and other overheads.

This is why the open source models are such a threat if they become good enough - it will destroy the business model of just providing raw chat/intelligence.

Arguably that's also why a few of these providers are trying to diversify into whole-platform approaches rather than just relying on having their whole thing be a great model.

comments.author: jeremyjh
comments.textZhHtml:
There has always been a lot of evidence that prices are only going down. The fact that you could already get DeepSeek or GLM inference from 20+ providers on openrouter.ai was already sufficient evidence that inference was profitable and being commoditized.

People that want to believe something different as a coping mechanism will not be swayed by this evidence either.

comments.author: jacquesm
comments.textZhHtml: AI will end up being a commodity. That's also why you already see the first rounds of protectionism under the guise of national security. Obviously they do have a point but that point works against them just as easily. Anybody that integrates unreviewed model output into their workflow is asking for trouble.

comments.textZhHtml: Either frontier AI will continue to get better steadily, until it's better than people at basically everything, and very weird things start to happen, or, it plateaus and the open weights models will eventually catch up.

comments.author: pegasus
comments.textZhHtml: There's a third possibility, which to me is also the most plausible.  Models will keep getting better and better within certain domains, while never catching up with humans when it comes to other type of tasks. Like that elusive quality-without-a-name some have called "taste". Or knowing what UX is most intuitive to humans. Really, anything where we have to tap into our common humanity and our human experience in order to be of help to other humans and generally to life on earth. Which is an all-important skill, since the flowering of life on the earth is (or should be) the whole point of anything we do, after all.

comments.textZhHtml: I don't know, that sounds like a question of taste. :)

comments.textZhHtml: ... as long as they still care about what we want and what we like.

comments.author: overfeed
comments.textZhHtml: Everyone knows the path followed by every single technology mankind has ever developed - including the incredible run that was Moore's law. Sure, some will think "This time is different" - but is it?

comments.author: Tuna-Fish
comments.textZhHtml: It doesn't need to run indefinitely. I don't think anyone sane thinks it's going to run indefinitely. It just needs to run long enough. Moore's law was what, 50 years? If AI keeps improving at the rate it currently is for 20 years, the world will be very different when that curve flattens out, in a way that makes most of our current concerns are entirely irrelevant.

comments.author: jacquesm
comments.textZhHtml:
Those cycles have shortened considerably. Just look at the lifespan of media, integrated circuits, software, products. There have been so many big model releases just in the last three months I've lost count. We're now closer to weeks between steps.

Maybe if China stops releasing capable models the pace will slow down a little, but they have lots of incentives not to.

comments.author: torginus
comments.textZhHtml:
It is, because just like you mentioned, there's no exponential physics to back up growth. LLMs have to stop scaling up compute, because there's only so much resources.

But even if we think back to the previous decade or two (sans AI), most of tech has been a a red queen's race - developing and improving stuff, without any real substantial results.

Microservices and orchestration are not better than old monoliths. Electron apps are not better than native. Most programs people actually use have decades-old codebases.

Video games of today don't look substantially better or play different than ones from 15 years ago.

stories.title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
stories.titleZh: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
stories.author: rzk
summaryZh: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...> I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like

comments.author: bitwizeshift
comments.textZhHtml:
I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created.

By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps.

The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes.

But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out.

It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

comments.author: davepeck
comments.textZhHtml:
A friend of mine sometimes jokes that code is “fractally busted” when it’s wrong at every level, from single lines all the way up to the design of the system’s main interfaces.

That’s also roughly what I find after a long English-only session with a coding agent. Our conversation covers a lot of ground... and leaves out details at every level. When I look at what got built, the misunderstandings are fractal too.

I agree it’s important to design it yourself, but UML is only one level. Lately I’ve been using a scratch Python file (or even a scratch repo) that Claude and I both edit. Never mind that I’m writing Rust. Python reads like pseudocode, and pass and ... (Ellipsis) let me skip whatever I don’t care about. At any level where I do care, I can say exactly what a method’s signature should look like, what fields a domain model should have, or how it should maintain key invariants. Everywhere else I leave an ellipsis, maybe a docstring, and let the agent decide.

It works both ways: I ask the agent to sketch the current system in Python, with some details elided and others spelled out. Then I edit the sketch and have the agent push the changes back into the much bigger Rust+Tauri app.

Time will tell whether this approach has legs, but when I want to be precise, I find it sometimes pays to just write some code.

comments.author: throwaway219450
comments.textZhHtml:
This is the way. I can write pseudo code (ie Python) and I leave a breadcrumb trail of comments where I want it to implement. Hell the code doesn’t even need to have valid syntax if you forgot some function signature, but that small amount of guiding can produce significantly better results than a blind implementation from the model.

I’ve also tried spending an hour or two first before handing over control. That way there’s something pre-existing it can work from.

comments.author: stickfigure
comments.textZhHtml:
I don't have this experience at all. My workflow is:

* Bite sized jobs, about what you would expect for a traditional user story.

* 10-15 minutes discussing the implementation. It's almost the exact same conversation I would have with a human engineer. I'm almost entirely asking questions - "How would you do Xyz? What about this problem? What about that problem?"

* At the end of the conversation, both the AI and I have a good understanding of the problem and the solution.

* I say "do it".

* There are occasions when I don't fully understand what it wants to do. I'll tell it to do the work, then we discuss it afterwards. Sometimes we change things, sometimes I just need to see the code to understand.

* It doesn't commit code. I do.

This has been really effective for me, easily 10X'd or more my pace of development. Sometimes I have to ask for a lot of rework and sometimes it one-shots it. But I never ship something I don't understand and it always feels like "my" code. Very satisfying. More satisfying than typing it all out; the typing was never the fun part of programming.

comments.author: zahlman
comments.textZhHtml:
I've found that current models will almost automatically sketch out some things in Python (or another suitable language for the type of task, or an implementation language you've already stipulated) while proposing a design, and you can go through a conversation of "what if we did xyz instead?" and at some point "okay, let's try writing a full prototype" (perhaps tacking on a bunch of decisions here so that things are resolved enough to work with).

But that's at the scale of <1kloc. Might be different if you're trying to do a bigger feature all at once.

comments.author: jasonjayr
comments.textZhHtml:
I suspect that's a problem both with human read/written code, and LLM written code -- larger features should be chunked up into more manageable to understand and reason about functions, and assembled at higher levels.

Guiding the LLM (or humans structuring/guiding juniors) to shape the abstractions help make the overall feature and reliability of the code much better.

stories.title: It's still ok to enjoy programming
stories.titleZh: It's still ok to enjoy programming
stories.author: goostavos
summaryZh: Published: 2026-10-17 Reading Hacker News makes me feel like I need to write this: it's still OK to enjoy programming. Yes, at work, where you are paid to produce value for a business, the economics of purely hand-written code have changed. But that's work. Work is not life. The loudest voices on the internet are the saddest and most infectious. To throw a tiny counter example in the sea of despair: I still program on the weekends because it is fun. I'm currently learning game programming! My current level of sophistication is a buggy Breakout clone with terrible collision detection. I write it by hand because I enjoy it. I struggle with problems because solving them makes me happy. It doesn't bother me that Claude could one-shot it, because that's not the point. I also get side-tracked from working on this "game" to study random programming topics. Last weekend was exploring how far I could push type safety in Java using ideas from dependently typed languages like Agda. There is no point to this. It gets tucked away under "interesting ways of thinking about a particular problem." Maybe it will come up in work life. Maybe not. I did it because exploring is was fun[0]. A few weekends ago: recursion schemes. Technically, this was not fun. I spent hours of banging my head against a wall. In the end, I still don't even know what's valuable about the ideas[1]. But I do know that many of the most beautiful ideas in programming only become clear to me after years of baking in my mind. It's why entire papers get written about Monoids. Maybe one day I'll find a problem that this applies to. Maybe not. I did it because understanding hard things is rewarding. I write this because I increasingly feel a strange social pressure. It's like I'm not "supposed" to enjoy this any more. As though there's no point or joy to be had in continuing to grow as a human. The more of this doom stream you consume, the more it starts to infect you. Maybe "there is no point," you find yourself thinking. But this disappears as soon as you disconnect.It's OK to enjoy things[2]. Doing so requires no economic justification. Footnotes: [0] Take the time to understand Fin one day. It is beautiful. [1] I'm not there yet, but the goal of studying this is to give myself another tool for reasoning about program correctness algebraically (a topic I cover in my book!) [2] I also have a blast vibe-coding. I've got a suite of apps for which I've never looked at a line of code. I suspect doing so would horrify me. "Programming" this way is also fun. Often extremely so. But in its own unique way.

comments.author: etra0
comments.textZhHtml:
Even if work is not life, hobby programming also has been affected.

I worked hard a couple of years ago to reverse engineer a game to produce a very specific tool. Recently, the game was updated, so I worked on my free time to do a free contribution to the community, and then, a few hours later a tool that does the same thing appeared entirely vibecoded.

Even if some parts of the community care about how a tool was made – Most don't, they just want something that fulfill the goal.

Now even my hobby programming was overtaken by AI, something I did for love and expected no pay out of it whatsoever, which is... depressing, to say the least.

comments.author: shoobiedoo
comments.textZhHtml:
I tried to look at it like cooking, or baking: I can make damn good croissants. They'll never be quite as good as someone with a dough sheeter and handmade cultured butter, but my friends and family would never complain.

The problem is, baking something and sharing it with others brings people together, there's smalltalk, catching up, other human stuff. Which in the end is kinda the point of it.

Like your post says, with programming, it's mostly just a race to what achieves the goal, with the exception of demoscene and retro programming, I guess. I started learning ARM assembly so I could make a lisp implementation in it. It will be useless, no one will use it, and an AI could bang one out in a few minutes, but overcoming that struggle to understand things in different ways has to be the goal with hobby programmers like myself, I guess.

comments.author: uludag
comments.textZhHtml:
I think this analogy breaks down in key areas. Software can be distributed limitlessly unlike a croissant, which can only be enjoyed by one peraon and only within a time period before it goea stale. stories.title: The 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement is no longer viable
stories.titleZh: The 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement is no longer viable
stories.author: velo_aprx
summaryZh: The target set in 2015 by the Paris Agreement—to limit global warming to 1.5°C by 2100—has become unachievable within the span of a single decade, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) notes in its 2026 Emissions Gap Report. “The opportunity to bridge the 1.5°C emissions gap with ‘no or limited’ overshoot has been lost,” states the report, titled “The Point of Return.” Exceeding the 1.5°C threshold above pre-industrial levels is now imminent and inevitable. New goal: not exceed 2°C, then bring the temperature back down to 1.5°C “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts,” the report states. The urgent task is to ensure that global warming remains below the 2°C threshold, with the aim of returning to 1.5°C by the end of the century. This is the only option left, according to UNEP.

© Maxim Tolchinskiy / Unsplash Highly inadequate climate plans To achieve this, global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions would need to be reduced by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. The current trajectory falls far short of this. Even assuming that the commitments made by governments—known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs)—are fully implemented, emissions would only be reduced by 5% to 8% by 2030 and by 11% to 15% by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The recommended efforts are “close to 6 per cent every single year until 2035,” declares the UN Secretary General. How can this be achieved? The UN Chief outlined the levers for action available to humanity: “The emissions gap is now a leadership gap. And the world is running out of time and excuses to close it. Governments must go much further and faster. Accelerate clean energy and electrification across every sector. Adopt credible roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels – with clear timelines and protection for affected workers and communities. Invest in grids and storage. Improve energy efficiency. Cut methane emissions. Halt and reverse deforestation.”

The physics, however, don’t change, and neither does the task in front of us.

I just spent ten months finding a job, the longest and most difficult job search of my career. It was hard because the macro environment is terrible, but also because I insisted on finding a role working on clean energy hardware.

At a time when basically all VC funding, and in many ways the entire productive capacity of the economy, is shifting to AI, it would have been smarter in some respects to just pivot to AI. I sat out the crypto bubble too, in which some of my peers made a lot of money by working on projects that were either useless, or straightforward scams.

We crossed the 1.5 degree threshold because the money can’t help itself. The slow, steady work of transitioning away from fossil fuels is never going to be as profitable, as quickly, as the various forms of gambling and addiction that have driven the tech industry for most of my lifetime.

But you, individually, can make the choice to keep your eye on the ball. You can commit to working on this problem until it’s done, no matter what. You can choose to find the others to organize and prepare, so that the ideas closest at hand when the next crisis comes are yours.

It’s the best solution I’ve come up with so far, and in spite of the challenges, it’s still working.

stories.title: What shall I teach my son?
stories.titleZh: What shall I teach my son?
stories.author: Curiositry
summaryZh: What is the purpose of education in the age of AGI? October 19, 2026 Yesterday, the title The End of Education by Neil Postman called to me from my bookshelf, whispering that it might be the right book at the right time. It was. Published in 1995, it was surprisingly appropriate balm for the soul of a confused programmer and soon-to-be father. My wife and I are expecting our first child. My economically valuable skillset – programming – suddenly feels less valuable. What shall I teach my son? And to what end?

Mr. Edison says That the radio will supplant the teacher. Already one may learn languages by means Of Victrola records. The moving picture will visualize What the radio fails to get across. Teachers will be relegated to the backwoods. With fire-horses, And long-haired women; Or, perhaps shown in museums. Education will become a matter Of pressing the button. Perhaps I can get a position at the switchboard. – Quoted in The End of Education by Neil Postman, quoting Teachers and Machines: The Use of Technology Since 1920 by Larry Cuban

comments.author: furyg3
comments.textZhHtml:
Parents should focus on enabling their children to be:

Curious; Resourceful; Self-reliant (to feel they have agency in the world); Compassionate; Value personal integrity, themselves, their ideas / wishes, and time on the planet; Able to cooperate, communicate, and work as a team; Able to make sacrifices for the future versions of themselves ("I'm having a bad day today, what can I do to make tomorrow me have a better day?"); Able to enjoy life and find fulfillment (however small) even in bad times.

School subjects, economies, social constructs, technology, they all change. A human who's motivated to develop themselves on topics like the above will be the best person they can be whether they are a CEO or living in a cave underground after an apocalypse.

comments.author: somenameforme
comments.textZhHtml:

Even if your brain was able to be scanned and then simulated atom by atom, your 'consciousness transferal' kit would be a brain scanner and a gun with one bullet.

So I think the answer is to first make yourself into somebody you're happy with, and then be yourself. Somebody who's happy with themselves is going to have a good life, regardless of how the world turns. And I think people who are happy with themselves also tend to be better humans to other people, regardless of all of these other terms and values we try to impose on this.

Like if somebody's belittling some service worker, it's not because of a lack of compassion, communication skills, emotional intelligence, or whatever else - it's because that person probably hates themselves, and they're taking out their own self loathing on others.

Shitty devs without AI are slowly building BS that wants to be cleaned up.

Shitty devs with AI are much more fasterly building BS that wants to be cleaned up.

I have a similar experience as yours, just add another 10-ish years to the timeline. Literally my first job out of uni, I got to work on a legacy code base that was another 15 years older than that which had a ton of reports all built differently over time with slight variations in both code and end user output that really all wanted to be "the same" both on the code and end user side. So I slowly but surely, one user/PM requested change at a time would build out a common layer of abstractions and shared code that both made the code shared and easier to maintain (great for me!) and consistent for users (great for the PM/users).

Heck, I built a rudimentary TransactSQL parser that'd output stored procedure call graphs to graphviz and then I printed it and hung it on the wall to get through all this and having an LLM to just make a mermaid out of this in 5-ish minutes would definitively have been faster than I was ;)

With an LLM all of that would just have been faster to do but still worthwhile and useful on both levels. I.e. both code abstraction/reuse and PM/user level. Similarly there was a report that one of the devs had to actually run manually and it took him a full week, so users that wanted the report would only request it once a year-ish. When I was asked to learn how to run it from him I was appalled and just took that week to put it into a script that we ran and emailed the report out once a month automatically. They ran that report manually like that for like 10 years prior to that :mindblown:

None of this is an "AI thing". It's a good dev vs. not so good dev thing. And none of it really has to do with coding as in "writing source code" as much as "solving problems for humans" somehow and the "language" you do that in changes over time. If you're the guy that's tied up with the particular language: yeah LLMs are gonna eat your lunch. If you're the problem solver type that uses whatever tools they have available, you're still in demand.
